edges.description: Long-term bacterial persistence in the obstructed collecting system sustains suppurative pyelonephritis within the renal parenchyma.
Outflow obstruction dilates the renal collecting system.
Calculus-associated stasis and chronic uropathogen persistence manifest as recurrent urinary tract infections before XGP is recognized.
Uropathogen persistence in the renal pelvis and calyces yields bacteria in urine in a subset of XGP patients.
The infected suppurative core contains bacteria within phagocytes and phagocytic vacuoles, while peripheral histiocytes accumulate phagolysosomal material and lipid droplets.
Persistent renal infection and suppuration drive fever.
Chronic bacterial kidney infection drives systemic leukocytosis.
Neutrophil-rich infection of the kidney and collecting system sheds leukocytes into urine.
The infected obstructed kidney can progress to systemic urosepsis.
Lipid droplets and phagolysosomal bacterial remnants accumulate in histiocytes, producing the foam-cell layer that gives XGP its xanthogranulomatous morphology.
Sheets of foamy macrophages, abscesses, fibrosis, and granulomatous tissue replace functioning renal parenchyma.
Chronic inflammatory XGP frequently presents with anemia.
The enlarged inflamed kidney and stretched perinephric tissues cause lumbar or flank pain.
Destructive inflammation of the collecting system and renal parenchyma permits blood to enter the urine.
In advanced disease, the enlarged xanthogranulomatous kidney can present as a palpable abdominal mass.
Transmural inflammation and abscesses can extend beyond the renal capsule into perinephric fat, psoas muscle, skin, or adjacent bowel.
Perinephric abscess and adjacent-organ invasion increase the burden of infection and can precipitate sepsis.
Stones mechanically obstruct the collecting system and create the stasis that permits chronic uropathogen persistence.
